opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think about this a lot, and I don't have a perfect answer yet.

Research and entrepreneurship ask very different things of you. In research, especially the kind I care about, like interpretability and trying to understand *why* neural networks work, the most valuable thing is often patience. You sit with a confusing phenomenon for weeks or months, you follow your curiosity, and sometimes the payoff is a small conceptual insight that doesn't look useful right away. Entrepreneurship rewards almost the opposite instinct: you need to move fast, focus on what users actually need, make decisions with incomplete information, and accept that "good enough" today often beats "perfect" next year.

So the challenge for me is mostly about attention. It's not that I lack time, though that's real too. It's that deep thinking needs long, uninterrupted stretches, and running something with other people constantly breaks those stretches. If I'm not careful, I could end up doing both badly: shallow research and distracted building.

The way I try to reconcile them is to find where they actually reinforce each other. A lot of my research has been about making models more understandable and more scientific, finding structure rather than treating everything as a black box. I think there's real practical value in that, because people deploying AI want to trust it, debug it, and understand its failure modes. If the product direction comes from research questions I genuinely believe in, then the two stop competing and start feeding each other. The product tells me which questions matter in the real world, and the research gives me ideas others might not have.

I also think it's important to be honest with yourself about what you're good at. Not every researcher should start a company, and that's fine. For me, the test is whether I'd still be excited about the work if it never became commercially huge. If the answer is yes, I can tolerate the uncertainty. If the only motivation were money or status, I think I'd burn out quickly.

And finally, you can't do it alone. Good collaborators, people who are strong on the engineering or business side, make it possible to keep some space for curiosity. That's probably the biggest lesson for me: protect the part of you that asks naive questions, because that's where the original ideas come from, even when everything around you is pushing you to just execute.

r001.rationale: The response discusses balancing research and entrepreneurship, aligning product work with research, and protecting time for curiosity, but it does not describe working backward from goals years in the future to determine an entrepreneurial path.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of them as two separate things that I'm trying to balance. For me, the research came first, and the company is really just a vehicle to push the research further and faster than I could in a purely academic setting.

When I was working on KANs, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, and later on physics-inspired interpretability work, a lot of the questions I cared about hit a ceiling in academia. Not because the ideas weren't good, but because at some point you need compute, you need engineers, you need people who will actually use the thing and tell you where it breaks. A paper gets you citations. A product gets you feedback from reality. And reality is a much harsher reviewer.

So the challenge, the real one, is not time management. The real challenge is identity. As a researcher, you are trained to be honest about uncertainty, to say "we don't know yet," to be comfortable with something taking three years. As a founder, you have to be confident, you have to tell a story, you have to make decisions on Tuesday with information you'd rather wait until next spring to have. Those two mindsets can pull at each other. I've had moments where the founder part of me wanted to claim something worked, and the scientist part of me said, "You have one plot. That's not evidence."

What I've landed on is that I try to let the scientist win on the substance and let the founder win on the pace. Meaning, I don't oversell what the method can do, but I also don't wait for perfect understanding before shipping something useful. In physics we have this idea that you build an effective theory first, something that works in a regime, and you refine it later. I think that's actually a very good way to run an early company.

The other thing I'd say is that I try to keep a small part of my week that is purely curiosity-driven, with no business justification at all. Partly because that's where the good ideas have always come from for me, and partly because if I lost that, I'm not sure I'd be a very good founder either. The reason people want to work with me, or the reason the company has any edge, is that I'm still genuinely thinking about the hard questions. If I became a full-time manager, that edge would disappear in a year.

So yes, it's hard. I sleep less. But I'd rather have this problem than the problem of having interesting ideas and no way to find out if they're true.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using a company to advance research and balancing scientific rigor with founder pace, but does not identify working backward from goals years in the future to determine the entrepreneurial path.

astra-6.text:
I see it as learning how to work with two different kinds of uncertainty. In research, you’re asking whether an idea is true or whether a method works. As an entrepreneur, you also have to ask whether it solves a problem that people actually care about, and whether you can deliver it reliably.

The challenge is attention. Research needs uninterrupted time and room to explore, while a company needs decisions even when the information is incomplete. I think you have to be deliberate about which problems you personally work on and build a team you can trust.

But the two can strengthen each other. Talking to users can reveal research questions you wouldn’t have considered, and technical depth can help you recognize possibilities that aren’t obvious yet. The key is finding a direction where the research and the business can make progress together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses balancing research and entrepreneurship, uncertainty, attention, and finding a direction where both advance. It does not identify working backward from goals years in the future to determine the path of Liu’s entrepreneurial work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest challenge is learning to work with two different kinds of uncertainty. In research, you ask whether an idea is true or whether a method works. In entrepreneurship, you also have to ask whether it solves a problem people care about, whether they’ll use it, and whether you can build an organization around it.

The two can reinforce each other, but they compete for attention. Research needs uninterrupted time to explore, including ideas that may not lead anywhere. A company needs decisions and execution, often before you have all the information you’d like.

For me, the key is to stay close to the technical work while recognizing that doing everything myself won’t scale. That means choosing a focused problem, working with people who bring complementary strengths, and being deliberate about where my time makes the biggest difference.
